chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
'God, Mighty and Majestic, is saying: [40:60] "Surely those who are too proud to worship Me shall soon enter Hell abased."'
He said: 'It (worship) is the supplication, and the most superior of the acts of worship is the supplication.'
I said: '[9:114] "Most surely Ibrahim was very tender-hearted, forbearing."'
He said: 'The tender-hearted one (awwah) — that is the one who supplicates much.'

key_terms.الدَّعَّاء: Daa'a — intensive form: one who supplicates very much (intensive form of daa'a)
key_terms.الدُّعَاء: Du'a — supplication and invocation; here defined as the very essence of worship ('ibada)
key_terms.الْأَوَّاه: Awwah — one who sighs or cries much; here reinterpreted as 'one who supplicates much' (daa'a)
key_terms.الْعِبَادَة: Worship ('ibada) — here interpreted by the Imam as referring specifically to du'a
key_terms.دَاخِرِينَ: Dakhirin — abased, humiliated, brought low (entering Hell in a state of disgrace)

ai.seo_question: Is du'a (supplication) the most superior act of worship in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) interprets two Quranic verses to establish the supreme status of du'a (supplication). He first cites Q 40:60, where God threatens with hellfire those too arrogant to worship, and declares that 'worship' here refers to du'a. He further explains that the Quranic description of Ibrahim as 'awwah' (tender-hearted/sighing) in Q 9:114 refers to Ibrahim's constant supplication to God. This hadith grounds du'a as the very essence of worship — the act that defines the worshipper's relationship with the divine. The original audience, Zurara and companions of the fifth Imam, would have understood this as an authoritative Imamic interpretation overriding merely linguistic readings of the Quran.
